reason: Corroborated by seven sources across multiple independent news and research sites covering discovery, flyby distance, and planetary defense implications.
story: On July 13, 2023, a 200-foot-wide asteroid designated 2023 NT1 swept past Earth at just one-quarter of the distance to the Moon. Large enough to cause catastrophic local devastation, the space rock flew completely undetected past our planet. It approached from the daytime sky, concealed entirely within the intense glare of the Sun. Early-warning systems remained blind until two days after the closest encounter, when an ATLAS telescope in South Africa finally spotted the asteroid leaving our cosmic neighborhood. The close call echoed the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor, which also sneaked in from the solar blind spot and injured roughly 1,500 people. While 2023 NT1 missed us, the incident prompted astronomers to model emergency defense proposals, such as hypervelocity interceptor arrays designed to pulverize surprise impactors on less than twenty-four hours of warning.
angle: A skyscraper-sized asteroid slipped past Earth closer than the Moon, and astronomers only realized it two days after it passed because it approached directly out of the Sun's glare.

claims.claim: Asteroid 2023 NT1 made a close flyby of Earth on July 13, 2023.
The asteroid passed within approximately one-quarter of the distance between Earth and the Moon.
Astronomers did not discover 2023 NT1 until July 15, two days after its closest approach.
The asteroid approached Earth from the direction of the Sun, remaining obscured by solar glare.
The initial detection was made by an ATLAS observatory telescope in South Africa.
ATLAS stands for Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System.
Asteroid 2023 NT1 has an estimated size of up to 60 meters (approximately 200 feet) across.
The asteroid made its closest approach to Earth at approximately 10:12 UTC on July 13, 2023.
2023 NT1 was substantially larger than the meteor that entered Earth's atmosphere over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 2013.
The 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor also went undetected prior to impact because it arrived from the direction of the Sun.
The 2013 Chelyabinsk explosion shattered windows and damaged structures, injuring roughly 1,500 people.
A direct atmospheric impact by 2023 NT1 could have caused significant local damage or destroyed an entire city.
The European Space Agency is developing the NEOMIR mission to detect asteroids hidden within solar glare.
The NEOMIR spacecraft is scheduled to launch around 2030 and orbit at the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point.
Planetary defense researchers published a study modeling a short-warning mitigation concept called Pulverize It to fragment similar surprise asteroids.

disputed: Asteroid velocity: S2 quotes NASA estimating 53,000 mph (86,000 km/h), S5 reports 25,000 mph, and S7 calculates 11.27 km/s at closest approach and 15.59 km/s entry velocity; scripts should omit exact speed figures or attribute them specifically to orbital models.

Exact diameter: Media reports state up to 60 meters (200 feet), while technical analysis in S7 gives a most probable diameter of 34 meters (range 26-58 meters) and S1 notes approximately 30 meters; scripts should present the measurement as a range up to 200 feet.
Chelyabinsk casualty figures: S2, S3, and S4 cite roughly 1,500 people injured, while S5 reports over 1,600; scripts should attribute the count broadly as around 1,500 people.
